FLASH proton radiation with or without gilvetmab for canine glioma

Penn Vet Ryan Veterinary Hospital · USA

Recruiting

What is being offered: Dogs need histopathologic confirmation of glioma or diagnostic MRI showing a supratentorial lesion consistent with glioma, must be suitable for general anesthesia, and must have a tumor compatible with the FLASH equipment. Systemic chemotherapy or immunotherapy requires a three-week washout; prior gilvetmab is not allowed. All dogs receive three FLASH proton treatments and are randomized to receive or not receive three gilvetmab infusions, with 12 follow-up visits over 11 months.

Who may qualify: Confirmed cancer diagnosis required; Active tumor required

May not qualify if: Prior gilvetmab; Anesthesia contraindicated

Costs / coverage: 🟡 Partially funded. Owners pay screening diagnostics; after enrollment the sponsor covers three FLASH-RT treatments, examinations, laboratory tests, sedation/anesthesia, CSF taps, gilvetmab infusions and protocol CT/MRI imaging.

Contact: Penn Vet VCIC — 215-573-0302; vcic@vet.upenn.edu

A listing here does not mean every pet will qualify. Enrollment can change, and the study team makes the final decision after reviewing your pet’s diagnosis, records and previous treatment.

# Clinical Trials for Dogs with Cancer

Links last verified: August 20, 2026

## Explore Current Research Trials in Canine Oncology

When a beloved dog is diagnosed with cancer, many families ask whether a clinical trial may provide an additional option. Canine oncology studies are conducted throughout the United States and around the world, but identifying an appropriate trial, and participating in one, can sometimes be challenging.

Each clinical trial has specific eligibility requirements.

These may include: 

  * A dog’s breed
  * Age
  * Weight
  * Overall health
  * Life expectancy
  * Cancer type
  * Cancer stage
  * Previous care
  * ...and other medical factors

Meeting a study’s general description does not guarantee acceptance. Pet parents should speak directly with the research team and their veterinary care provider to determine whether a trial may be appropriate for their dog.

It is also important to understand that clinical trials are not always free.

Research funding may cover only certain tests, medications, procedures, or appointments. Families may still be responsible for additional veterinary expenses, travel, lodging, and repeated visits over several weeks or months, especially when a study is located far from home.

The following links are intended to help pet parents and veterinary professionals find information about current canine oncology trials being conducted throughout the United States and, in some cases, internationally.

We encourage families to carefully review each study’s eligibility requirements, location, potential costs, time commitment, and possible benefits and risks with their veterinary team.

## Start Here: Nationwide Search Tools

If you are not sure where to begin, start with the AVMA registry. It lets you search by cancer type and by location, which is faster than checking individual centers one at a time.

#### AVMA Veterinary Clinical Trials Registry

The AVMA Veterinary Clinical Trials Registry, formerly known as the AVMA Animal Health Studies Database, helps dog parents and veterinary professionals find veterinary clinical studies taking place throughout the United States and Canada. By making this information easier to access, the registry supports continued research and progress in veterinary medicine and canine health care.

If you are interested in a clinical trial for your dog, begin by discussing the study and your dog’s potential eligibility with your veterinary care provider.

 

AVMA Clinical Trials

#### National Cancer Institute, Comparative Oncology Program

The Comparative Oncology Program develops and conducts clinical trials in partnership with veterinary teaching institutions throughout the United States. Dogs enrolled in these studies receive care from board-certified veterinary oncologists committed to improving comfort, quality of life, and cancer care for companion animals.

The knowledge gained through this research may help advance the understanding of cancer and support future progress in both canine and human oncology.

National Cancer Institute

#### PetCure Oncology

PetCure Oncology provides stereotactic radiation surgery and stereotactic radiation therapy, commonly known as SRS and SRT. These highly precise forms of radiation therapy have been used in human oncology and are now available for dogs with certain types of cancer.

PetCure Oncology reports using SRS and SRT in thousands of companion animals with a variety of tumor types. Its affiliated veterinary specialists continue to study these approaches to better understand their potential benefits, safety considerations, side effects, and appropriate applications in canine cancer care.

PetCure Oncology Clinical Trials

#### ACI Biosciences

Network conducting trials at participating private practices.

ACI Biosciences Clinical Trials

## Our Services

The VCIC works closely with corporate sponsors, individual clinicians, clients, and patients, offering services ranging from recruitment, study design, protocol compliance, quality assurance, data capture, and reporting, conducting clinical trials at both Penn Vet hospitals.

### Targeted Marketing & Recruitment Strategies

The VCIC has demonstrated an ability to recruit significant sample sizes in a wide array of disease models over more than 14 years of managing veterinary clinical trials. Ryan Hospital’s large case load combined with its extensive referral network of more than 3,000 veterinary practices make it uniquely suited for clinical trial recruitment and enrollment.
When a trial requires more animals with a specific condition than would normally be presented in the 34,000 pets that come to Ryan Hospital annually, the VCIC has a proven record for targeted recruitment of animals at over 400 percent above baseline presentation rate.
VCIC understands and employs recruitment modalities that are most effective for a given target population and can guide sponsors on the most efficient means to enroll the desired number of animals in a specified period of time for a given study, pain management, and disease specific recommendations.

# Open Clinical Trials

The Comparative Oncology Program (COP) designs and implements clinical trials in collaboration with academic veterinary institutions across the United States. Pet animals will receive treatment under the care of board-certified veterinary oncologists who share our goal of alleviating the suffering of companion animals with cancer. Information gained by the clinical trials will be used to benefit both animals and humans with cancer.

### COTC029: Pilot assessment of BG34-200 in spontaneous canine cancers

The purpose of this study is to evaluate dose escalation of BG34-200 in dogs with cancer. We will 1) evaluate the safety of BG34-200, and 2) evaluate the ability of BG34-200 to stimulate a patient’s immune system to detect and destroy cancer cells.

Learn More

### COTC033: Repurposing vaccine immunity to treat cancers: validation in canine patients

This clinical trial, led by the National Cancer Institute (NCI), in collaboration with Dr. John T. Schiller, assesses the safety and effectiveness of intra-tumoral administered vaccines, when given to dogs with cancer.

### Bladder Cancer Study

Contact:
Samuel Stewart
sstewart@ethosvet.com

##### Pilot study to evaluate the safety and pharmacodynamic effects of a fully canine anti-PD1 antibody in pet dogs with urothelial carcinoma

Dogs with urothelial carcinoma may be eligible to participate in a clinical trial. This study seeks to evaluate a novel immunotherapy that specifically targets an important molecule primarily expressed on immune cells. This molecule usually turns off the immune cells and prevents overactive immune responses. However, it also turns off anti-cancer immune responses and prevents the immune system controlling and killing cancer cells. Immunotherapies that can inhibit this molecule on immune cells that recognize cancer cells could make it possible for the immune system to recognize and attack the underlying cancer more effectively. This study seeks to evaluate the tolerability and efficacy of this novel immunotherapy in dogs with urothelial carcinoma.

### Details of Study
Study Type   | Interventional 
Intervention   | Drug 
Inclusion Criteria  | 

  * Weigh ≥5kg and ≤35kg
  * Histologically confirmed urothelial carcinoma, with or without documented lymph node involvement (both newly diagnosed dogs and those with recurrent/relapsed disease are eligible)
  * Measurable tumor burden with primary intravesicular tumor amenable for cystoscopic biopsy
  * ECOG performance status of grade 0 or 1
  * Adequate hematologic, hepatic, and renal function
  * Creatinine ≤2.0 mg/dL
  * No significant comorbidities
  * Expected survival time of at least eight weeks
  * Signed informed owner consent
Exclusion Criteria   | 

  * Body weight of <5kg or >35kg
  * Pulmonary metastatic disease
  * History of any diagnosed or suspected autoimmune or immune-mediated disease, colitis, IBD, endocrine disorders
  * Significant comorbidities
  * Symptomatic urinary tract infection confirmed on urine culture
  * Any >grade 2 hematologic or biochemical abnormality
  * History of daily drug administration for unregulated chronic disease

# Veterinary Clinical Trials

Clinical trials at VROC help evaluate new cancer treatments for pets by assessing their safety, effectiveness, and potential side effects. Participation is entirely voluntary, and the decision to enroll your pet is yours. However, enrollment in a clinical trial is required for a patient to be seen in our clinic.

Our studies build upon the current standard of care using the same advanced technologies available in leading specialty pet cancer hospitals. While specific outcomes cannot be guaranteed, our team is committed to providing the highest standard of veterinary oncology care throughout each trial.

For questions or to learn more about available studies, please contact Paige Neumann, Research Study Coordinator, at 214-645-6221 or by VROC@UTSouthwestern.edu (no-reply@utsouthwestern.edu).

## Clinical Trials Now Enrolling

#### CALL FOR PATIENTS: Clinical Trial for Soft Tissue Sarcoma in Dogs

Study Title: Feasibility and dose-optimization clinical trial of local immunotherapy for solid tumors in canine cancer patients

Eligibility: Any dog weighing 5kg or above with at least one cutaneous soft tissue sarcoma lesion that is greater than 1.7cm in diameter is eligible to enroll. All dogs that meet the study criteria will receive the study drug (no placebo) followed by surgical removal of the tumor 1 week later.

Study Purpose: This clinical trial evaluates the safety, feasibility, and biological effects of a newly designed immunotherapy. Specifically, the study is evaluating the injection of investigational T-cell engagers (TCEs) directly into tumors (intratumorally) in canine patients with soft tissue sarcoma (STS). TCEs are engineered antibodies that physically connect T cells to cancer cells by targeting specific markers (CD3 or CD28 on T cells, and B7-H3 or PD-L1 on cancer cells), triggering the immune system to destroy tumor cells.

# Advancing Canine Brain Tumor Treatment

Image: A black and white Boston Terrier on an exam table

## What We Do

The Canine Brain Tumor Program provides advanced clinical care for dogs while accelerating human brain tumor research.

## About the program

The University of Minnesota Canine Brain Tumor Program is a multifaceted, internationally recognized program that advances care for both dogs and people affected by primary brain tumors. We provide cutting-edge therapy to dogs to preserve their quality of life and improve long-term survival. We study how canine and human gliomas are similar to each other, so that the clinical trials we conduct benefit both dogs and people. Our trials are supported by a variety of financial sponsors, including grants from foundations and government agencies. The majority of costs associated with enrollment are covered through these funding mechanisms.

## Join our clinical trials

Enroll now

## Collaborate with us

The CBTP partners with scientific organizations conducting cutting edge clinical research. Our goal is to unite canine brain tumor patients with innovative diagnostic and treatment options. To learn more about collaborating with the CBTP, please contact us at [email protected].

See all current clinical trials in the Clinical Investigation Center.

Research ethics at the University of Minnesota. We are committed to protecting research participants, upholding ethical standards, and improving our practice at every step of our work.

## Study title

Engaging the Immune System to Kill Solid Tumors in Pet Dogs - A Comparative Oncology Approach (TriKE + Radiation Therapy)

## Purpose of study

The purpose of the study is to identify a safe and effective dose of a novel immunotherapy drug (TriKE) when given with hypofractionated radiation therapy (RT) in companion dogs with a sarcoma. 

## Eligibility criteria

Dogs must: 

  * Have cytologically or histopathologicaly confirmed sarcoma, measuring at least 2cm
  * Weigh at least 7 kg (15 lbs)
